title: ph and wh, and the Two Sounds of c and g
overview:
New spellings: ph, wh.
Two spellings that say something other than they look.
Two letters. One sound.
Do not sound them out one by one.
functions: Say the sound for each new spelling
Read a word that has one in it
Write a word that has one in it
Know where in a word each one goes
Read the new words out loud
Choose between two spellings of one sound
learningPath: Words: the new spellings and the new words.
Write the words from their sounds.
Practice and quiz. Check your answers.
lectureScript:
This is Unit 19. Two spellings and two letters.
First, ph. Look at it. P and h.
But it does not say p. It does not say h.
It says f.
Phone. ph. o_e. n. Three sounds.
Not p-hone. Fone.
Photo. Graph. All the f sound.
There are not many. Learn them as you meet them.
Next, wh. White. When. Where. Why.
It is very close to w on its own.
Most people say them the same now.
What matters is that you know it is one spelling.
And here is the useful part.
Nearly every question word starts with wh.
What. When. Where. Why. Which. Who.
See wh at the start and it is often a question.
Now the two letters. C and g.
You know c as in cat. That is the hard c.
But listen to this word. City.
City. The c says s.
Cent. Ice. Face. All the s sound.
When does that happen? There is a rule.
Before e, i or y, the c says s.
Cat, cup, cot. Hard c. A, u, o after it.
City, cent, cycle. Soft c. E, i, y after it.
Now g. You know g as in got. The hard g.
Listen. Age. Page. Giant.
The g says j.
Same rule. Before e, i or y, g often says j.
Only often. Get and give are hard.
So try the hard one, then the soft one.
One last thing about the letter y.
At the start it is a sound. Yes.
At the end of a short word it is long i. My.
At the end of a longer word it is long e.
City. Very. Happy. Only.
Three jobs for one letter.
That is Unit 19. One unit left.

grammar.title: The new spellings: ph, wh
grammar.explanation:
These spellings do not say what they look like.
ph says f. And c and g each have two sounds.
There are rules here, and they mostly hold.
grammar.rule:
ph   as in phone   says f
wh   as in white   at the start

c    cat  hard     city  soft, says s
g    got  hard     age   soft, says j
grammar.workedExample:
You see ph in a word.
1. Do not read two letters.
2. Read one sound.
3. Say that sound out loud.
4. Now find it in phone.
5. Say the sound again there.
grammar.mistake:
Sounding out both letters gives no word at all.
phone is not p - h - o - n - e.
It is ph - o_e - n.
grammar.tip: Two letters. Look once. Say once.
grammar.practice:
Say the sound for each one.
1. ph
2. wh
grammar.answers:
Check yourself out loud.
Did you say ONE sound each time?
Two sounds means you read the letters, not the spelling.

grammar.title: Reading a word that has ph, wh in it
grammar.explanation:
Find the two letters first.
Read them as one sound.
Then read the rest of the word.
grammar.rule:
phone    ph - o_e - n
white    wh - i_e - t
wheel    wh - ee - l
city     c - i - t - y
cent     c - e - n - t
age      a_e - g
grammar.workedExample:
You see the word white.
1. Look for the two letters.
2. Cover them with your finger.
3. Read what is left.
4. Now put the one sound back in.
5. Join it all. white.
grammar.mistake:
Reading left to right, letter by letter, breaks here.
Look for the pair BEFORE you start.
grammar.practice:
Join the sounds and write the word.
1. ph - o_e - n
2. wh - i_e - t
3. wh - ee - l
4. c - i - t - y
5. c - e - n - t
6. a_e - g
grammar.answers:
1. phone
2. white
3. wheel
4. city
5. cent
6. age
Five or six right? You can read these.

grammar.title: Writing a word that has ph, wh in it
grammar.explanation:
Say the word. Break it into sounds.
One of those sounds needs TWO letters.
Count sounds, then write.
grammar.rule:
phone    ph - o_e - n       3 sounds, 5 letters
white    wh - i_e - t       3 sounds, 5 letters
grammar.workedExample:
You want to write wheel.
1. Say it out loud.
2. Break it: wh - ee - l.
3. Which sound needs two letters?
4. Write that pair together.
5. Read it back to check.
grammar.mistake:
One letter for each sound is wrong now.
The new sound takes two letters.
grammar.tip: Count sounds. Some need two letters.
grammar.practice:
Write the word you hear.
1. wheel
2. city
3. cent
4. age
5. page
6. giant
grammar.answers:
1. wheel
2. city
3. cent
4. age
5. page
6. giant
Five or six right? Good.

grammar.title: c and g each have two sounds
grammar.explanation:
Before e, i or y, c says s.
Before e, i or y, g often says j.
Everywhere else they are hard.
grammar.rule:
hard c    cat, cup, cot, cross
soft c    city, cent, ice, face

hard g    got, gas, bag, grow
soft g    age, page, giant, large

c is reliable. g is only usually.
grammar.workedExample:
You see the word cent.
1. Find the c. It is first.
2. Look at the letter after it.
3. It is an e.
4. So the c says s.
5. s - e - n - t. Cent.
grammar.mistake:
Reading city with a hard c gives kitty.
Look at the next letter before you say the c.
grammar.tip: e, i or y after it? Then it is soft.
grammar.practice:
Hard or soft? Say each one out loud.
1. cat
2. city
3. got
4. age
5. cup
6. page
grammar.answers:
1. hard
2. soft
3. hard
4. soft
5. hard
6. soft
The soft ones all have e, i or y after the letter.

grammar.title: The letter y has three jobs
grammar.explanation:
You have met two of them already.
Here is the third, and it is the commonest.
Where the y sits tells you which.
grammar.rule:
at the start        yes, yet, yard     its own sound
end of a short word my, try, why       long i
end of a long word  city, very, happy  long e

One letter. Three jobs.
grammar.workedExample:
You see the word only.
1. Where is the y? At the end.
2. Is the word short or long?
3. It has two beats. On-ly.
4. So the y says long e.
5. Only. Not on-lie.
grammar.mistake:
Every final y read as long i gives vur-eye.
Count the beats in the word first.
grammar.tip: Short word, long i. Long word, long e.
grammar.practice:
What does the y say? Sound, long i, or long e?
1. yes
2. my
3. city
4. try
5. very
6. yard
grammar.answers:
1. sound
2. long i
3. long e
4. long i
5. long e
6. sound
The long e ones are the words with two beats.

readings.title: The Phone Call
readings.genre: A short text using known spellings
readings.setting: A morning at home, waiting for a call
readings.passage:
My phone rang at six.
It was a man from the city.
He said: when can you start?
I got on a white bus.
A wheel on the bus went flat.
I was late. The man did not care.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — The new sounds
speaking.instructions:
Listen and repeat each sound.
ph
wh
ONE sound each. Not two.
Now say each one three times.
Tap the mic. Say them all.
Check: one sound, or did two slip out?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to say one of the new sounds. Say it back.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Read the words
speaking.instructions:
Say each word two ways. Slow, then fast.
1. ph - o_e - n ... phone
2. wh - i_e - t ... white
3. wh - ee - l ... wheel
4. c - i - t - y ... city
5. c - e - n - t ... cent
6. a_e - g ... age
Tap the mic. Say all six both ways.
Check: was the new spelling one sound?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to say three sounds. Join them and say the word.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Say it, then write it
speaking.instructions:
For each word: say it, break it, write it.
1. wheel
2. city
3. cent
4. age
5. page
6. giant
Tap the mic. Say each word and its sounds.
Check: did you say the sounds before you wrote?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor for a word with the new spelling. Break it out loud.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Read the list
speaking.instructions:
Read these out loud, straight down the list.
phone
white
wheel
city
cent
age
page
giant
Do it twice. The second time, try not to stop.
Tap the mic. Read the list twice.
Check: was the second time easier?
speaking.tutor: Read the list to the tutor. Ask which words were not clear.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Hard and soft
speaking.instructions:
Say each word. Then say hard or soft.
cat. city. got. age. cup. page.
Look at the letter after the c or the g.
Tap the mic. Do all six.
Check: e, i or y after every soft one?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor for a word with a soft c in it.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Three jobs for y
speaking.instructions:
Say each word. Then say what the y does.
yes. my. city. try. very. yard.
Sound, long i, or long e.
Tap the mic. Do all six.
Check: were the long e ones the longer words?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor for a word ending in y with two beats.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Words with the new spelling
writing.prompt:

Write two letters for the new sound.
writing.criteria:

writing.extension: Now write one more word with the same spelling.

writing.title: Writing 2 — Sounds and letters
writing.prompt:

How many sounds. How many letters.
writing.criteria:
Six words.
Two numbers beside each one.
The numbers are not the same. That is the point.
writing.extension: Find a word where they ARE the same.

quizzes.q: When you see ph you should ___.
quizzes.why: Read the pair as one, not as two letters.

quizzes.q: Join the sounds: ph - o_e - n. The word is ___.
quizzes.why: The sounds in order make the word.

quizzes.q: Join the sounds: wh - i_e - t. The word is ___.
quizzes.why: Find the pair first, then read the rest.

quizzes.q: To write a word with the new spelling you ___.
options: write two letters for that sound
write one letter for each sound
quizzes.a: write two letters for that sound
quizzes.why: The new sound is one sound and two letters.

quizzes.q: How many sounds are in phone?
quizzes.why: Count what you HEAR. There are more letters than sounds.

options: read the pair as one sound
quizzes.a: read the pair as one sound
quizzes.why: Letter by letter is the slow way here.

quizzes.q: You cannot read a word. What do you do first?
quizzes.why: Find the pair, then read around it.

quizzes.q: In the word city, the c says ___.
quizzes.why: Before e, i or y, the c says s.

quizzes.q: A c says s when the next letter is ___.
quizzes.why: Cat, cup and cot are hard. City and cent are soft.

quizzes.q: In the word city, the y at the end says ___.
quizzes.why: In a long word, the final y is long e.

quizzes.q: In the word my, the y says ___.
quizzes.why: At a short word's end, y is long i.

teacherNotes.note: Every pattern card has a worked example, every practice has a key, and every speaking task ends with record, listen back, check.

This is the whole unit, and it goes against everything Units 2 to 7 taught. Expect a learner to read the letters separately for a while. Do not explain it again; point at the pair and say the one sound, and have them say it back. It is a habit, and habits are built by repetition, not by argument.

teacherNotes.type: Find the pair before reading, not during
teacherNotes.note: Left-to-right letter-by-letter reading breaks on these words, because the learner commits to the first letter's sound before they have seen the second. The move is to scan the word for the pair first. A finger under the pair is enough. It looks like a crutch and it is the skill.

From here to the end of the level there are always more letters than sounds. A learner who counts letters will write a spare letter into every word. Have them say the word and count on their fingers before they write.

teacherNotes.type: The soft c rule is reliable. The soft g rule is not
teacherNotes.note: c before e, i or y is soft every time a learner will meet. g is soft in age and hard in get, give, girl and gift, all of them common. Teach c as a rule and g as a first guess with a fallback: try soft, and if it is not a word try hard. Presenting them as one rule produces a learner who reads get as jet.

teacherNotes.type: wh barely differs from w in speech, and that is fine
teacherNotes.note: Most speakers no longer distinguish them. Do not drill a difference the learner will never hear outside the lesson. What is worth teaching is the pattern: what, when, where, why, which, who — nearly every question word starts wh, and spotting that at the start of a sentence is genuinely useful.

teacherNotes.type: y saying long e is the commonest y of all
teacherNotes.note: City, very, happy, only, many, money, family, body. It is everywhere, and a learner who only has the long i will read all of them wrongly. The beat count is the test: one beat means long i, more than one means long e. It is not perfect but it is right almost every time.

assignment.title: Read and write the new words
assignment.instructions:
Two parts.
1. Record yourself. Say the sound for each new spelling.
Then read these words, slowly and then faster:
phone, white, wheel, city, cent, age
2. Write six of the words from their sounds.
Beside each one, write how many sounds it has.
Listen back before you finish.
